questions.stem: Converting information into a form that can be stored in memory is called:
options: encoding
retrieval
consolidation
decay
questions.explanation: Encoding converts sensory information into a usable form for storage. Storage is holding it over time, and retrieval is getting it back out.

questions.stem: A shopper's eyes register hundreds of items on a shelf, but only the cereal she looks for reaches short-term memory. In the multi-store model, what moves it there?
options: maintenance rehearsal
consolidation
retrieval
selective attention
questions.explanation: Selective attention determines which information in sensory memory is transferred to short-term memory. Unattended information quickly decays.

questions.stem: Which comparison of sensory memory and short-term memory is correct?
options: Sensory memory holds only meaningful information; STM holds only raw sensations
Sensory memory holds a lot for seconds or less; STM holds about 7 items for up to 30 s
Sensory memory holds about 7 items for a minute; STM holds a lot for a fraction of a second
Both hold an unlimited amount of information for an unlimited length of time
questions.explanation: Sensory memory has a large capacity but holds information very briefly (iconic about 0.2 to 0.5 seconds, echoic about 3 to 4 seconds). STM holds about 7 ± 2 items for roughly 18 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.

questions.stem: Repeating a phone number over and over to keep it in mind until you dial it is:
options: elaborative rehearsal
chunking
consolidation
maintenance rehearsal
questions.explanation: Maintenance rehearsal is simple repetition that keeps information active in short-term memory. Elaborative rehearsal links information to existing knowledge and is better for long-term storage.

questions.stem: A student learns new biology terms by linking each to examples from her own life. Why will this produce better long-term recall than repeating the terms aloud?
options: Maintenance rehearsal keeps the terms in sensory memory for much longer
Repeating terms aloud transfers them straight into long-term memory
Linking to examples reduces the amount of information to be stored
Elaborative rehearsal encodes meaning, giving more retrieval links
questions.explanation: Elaborative rehearsal involves processing meaning and connecting new information to existing knowledge, so it is more deeply encoded and has more retrieval cues.

questions.stem: Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model replaced the single short-term store with several components. Which component holds and rehearses speech-based information?
options: the central executive
the episodic buffer
the phonological loop
the visuo-spatial sketchpad
questions.explanation: The phonological loop holds sounds and words and rehearses them with an inner voice. The visuo-spatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information.

questions.stem: People find it hard to repeat a list of words aloud while also memorising another word list, but can repeat words while tracking a moving dot fairly easily. How does working memory explain this?
options: Word tasks compete for the phonological loop; the dot uses the sketchpad
The word tasks use different components, so they should be easy to combine
The central executive can only control one task at a time of any kind
The episodic buffer stores visual information but cannot store words
questions.explanation: Two tasks using the same component (the phonological loop) interfere with each other, while tasks using different components (loop and sketchpad) can be done together with less interference.

questions.stem: In the working memory model, the episodic buffer (added by Baddeley in 2000) is responsible for:
options: holding visual images and spatial layouts such as a route to school
holding sounds and words through an inner voice and an inner ear
combining information from the other components and long-term memory
directing attention and coordinating the other components of the model
questions.explanation: The episodic buffer is a limited-capacity store that integrates information from the phonological loop, the sketchpad and long-term memory into single episodes. Directing attention is the central executive's role.

questions.stem: Craik and Lockhart's levels of processing framework proposes that:
options: information must pass through three separate memory stores
memories fade with time if they are not regularly used
new learning interferes with recall of older learning
deeper, more meaningful processing leads to better recall
questions.explanation: Craik and Lockhart argued that memory depends on the depth of processing rather than on separate stores. Semantic (meaning-based) processing produces more durable memories than shallow processing.

questions.stem: In Craik and Tulving's (1975) study, participants answered questions about words. Which question would lead to the best later recall of the word 'tiger'?
options: Does the word contain exactly five letters?
Would the word fit the sentence 'The zookeeper fed the ___'?
Is the word printed in capital letters on the card?
Does the word rhyme with the word 'spider'?
questions.explanation: Questions requiring semantic processing (meaning) led to better recall than phonemic (rhyme) or structural (appearance) questions, supporting the levels of processing framework.

questions.stem: A woman can picture the cake, the guests and the rain at her 16th birthday party. Recalling this draws on her:
options: episodic memory
semantic memory
procedural memory
sensory memory
questions.explanation: Episodic memory is memory for personal experiences tied to a time and place. Semantic memory is general knowledge and facts, such as the capital of Australia.

questions.stem: After a brain injury, a man cannot recall facts about his own past, yet he still rides a bicycle and ties his shoelaces easily. Which kind of memory has been spared?
options: episodic memory
semantic memory
sensory memory
procedural memory
questions.explanation: Procedural memory is memory for how to perform skills and actions, often recalled without conscious awareness. Facts are semantic and personal events are episodic; both are declarative.

questions.stem: In Collins and Quillian's (1969) study, people took longer to verify 'A canary has skin' than 'A canary can sing'. How does semantic network theory explain this?
options: 'Has skin' is stored higher up, so more links must be travelled
'Has skin' is an episodic memory, so it is harder to retrieve
'Can sing' was rehearsed more often by the people in the study
'Can sing' is a procedural memory, so it is retrieved automatically
questions.explanation: In the hierarchical network, properties are stored at the most general level that applies (skin at 'animal', singing at 'canary'). Verifying 'has skin' requires moving up two levels, which takes longer.

questions.stem: Consolidation theory proposes that:
options: new information interferes with the recall of old information
memories are rebuilt each time they are retrieved from storage
new memories need time to be fixed into long-term storage
memories fade if they are not used over a period of time
questions.explanation: Consolidation is the process by which new memories become stable in long-term memory over time. If it is disrupted, for example by a head injury, recent memories may be lost.

questions.stem: A footballer is knocked unconscious and cannot remember the few minutes before the collision, though his older memories are intact. Which explanation fits best?
options: The memories were repressed because they were traumatic
The memories were displaced by newer information later on
The memories faded through decay over the following years
The memories had not been consolidated before the injury
questions.explanation: Memories of the minutes before the injury were still being consolidated, and the injury disrupted this, causing a short retrograde amnesia.

questions.stem: In Loftus and Palmer's (1974) study, participants who were asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates than those asked with 'hit'. This shows:
options: eyewitnesses always recall events with accuracy
the wording of a question can alter eyewitness memory
people cannot judge the speed of cars from a video
memories decay quickly if they are not rehearsed
questions.explanation: The verb used in a leading question altered speed estimates, showing that information given after an event can change memory of it. This has implications for police interviews.

questions.stem: A week later, more participants in Loftus and Palmer's 'smashed' group falsely reported seeing broken glass than in the 'hit' group. What does this suggest?
options: The film used in the smashed condition showed more broken glass
The participants were deliberately lying to please the researchers
The question changed the memory itself, not just the answer given
Participants in the smashed group had better memories of the film
questions.explanation: There was no broken glass in the film. Reporting it a week later suggests the misleading verb was integrated into the memory, supporting the reconstructive nature of memory.

questions.stem: In Bartlett's (1932) 'War of the Ghosts' study, British participants' retellings of a Native American folk tale became shorter and more conventional over time. This suggests that memory is:
options: an exact recording of what was heard
stored only in sensory memory stores
not affected by a person's culture
reconstructed using existing schemas
questions.explanation: Participants altered unfamiliar details to fit their own cultural schemas and expectations, showing that recall is an active reconstruction rather than a replay.

questions.stem: A person with memory impairment confidently describes a holiday that never happened, believing it to be true. This is:
options: repression
suppression
pseudo-forgetting
confabulation
questions.explanation: Confabulation is the unintentional production of false memories to fill gaps, without any intention to deceive. It is common in Korsakoff's syndrome.

questions.stem: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows that forgetting of nonsense syllables is:
options: absent for the first week, then sudden and complete
rapid soon after learning, then slows and levels off
slow at first, then speeds up rapidly over time
steady and constant at the same rate over time
questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus found most forgetting occurs within the first hour or so after learning; the rate then slows, and what remains after a few days is relatively stable.

questions.stem: Ebbinghaus measured retention with the method of savings. This involves:
options: counting the errors participants make on their very first attempt
comparing the time needed to relearn material with the time first needed
asking participants to recall as many items as possible without any cues
asking participants to pick the correct items from a list of options
questions.explanation: Savings is the reduction in the time or trials needed to relearn material compared with original learning. It detects memory even when recall is impossible.

questions.stem: A student cannot recall an actor's name, feels it is 'right there', and remembers it is two syllables starting with 'B'. This is:
options: motivated forgetting
decay theory
the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon
proactive interference
questions.explanation: The tip-of-the-tongue state shows that information is stored but cannot be retrieved without the right cue, which supports retrieval failure as a cause of forgetting.

questions.stem: Divers who learned word lists underwater recalled them better underwater than on land. This is an example of:
options: context-dependent forgetting
state-dependent forgetting
retroactive interference
pseudo-forgetting
questions.explanation: Context-dependent forgetting occurs when external cues present at learning are absent at recall. State-dependent forgetting depends on internal states, such as mood or intoxication.

questions.stem: A man changes his phone PIN, but for weeks he keeps typing the old one when he tries to unlock it. This is:
options: proactive interference
retroactive interference
repression
decay
questions.explanation: Proactive interference occurs when old learning disrupts recall of new learning. Retroactive interference is new learning disrupting recall of old learning.

questions.stem: A student studies French on Monday and Italian on Tuesday. On Wednesday her French test is worse than expected because Italian words keep coming to mind. This is:
options: decay theory
failure to encode
retroactive interference
proactive interference
questions.explanation: The later learning (Italian) is interfering with recall of earlier learning (French), which is retroactive interference. Similar material causes the most interference.

questions.stem: What is the difference between repression and suppression?
options: Repression affects only positive memories; suppression affects only negative
Repression is an organic cause; suppression is caused by brain damage
Repression is unconscious; suppression is a deliberate choice
Repression is a conscious choice; suppression happens without awareness
questions.explanation: Both are forms of motivated forgetting of distressing memories. Freud saw repression as an unconscious defence, while suppression is deliberately pushing a memory out of mind.

questions.stem: Which observation most challenges decay theory as a complete explanation of forgetting?
options: Forgetting increases as more time passes after learning
Unused skills sometimes become less fluent over time
Some memory traces fade if they are never retrieved
Old memories can return when the right cue is given
questions.explanation: If memories simply faded over time, they should not be recoverable. Their return with cues suggests they were still stored and that retrieval had failed.

questions.stem: Anterograde amnesia is:
options: an inability to form new long-term memories after damage
a loss of memories of events from before the brain damage
a deliberate attempt to push distressing memories out of mind
a gradual loss of all memories due to unused memory traces
questions.explanation: Anterograde amnesia prevents new information from being stored in long-term memory after the damage occurs. Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before the damage.

questions.stem: Korsakoff's syndrome is caused mainly by:
options: a lack of thiamine (vitamin B1), often due to chronic alcohol misuse
a build-up of amyloid plaques and tangles in the brains of older people
a single blow to the head during a sporting game or road accident
the deliberate suppression of memories of a stressful life event
questions.explanation: Korsakoff's syndrome results from thiamine deficiency, most often linked to long-term heavy drinking. It causes anterograde amnesia and confabulation.

questions.stem: Alzheimer's disease is associated with:
options: amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain
a deficiency of thiamine caused by heavy alcohol use
a single head injury causing a short retrograde amnesia
the motivated forgetting of distressing life events
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease marked by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, beginning with problems forming new memories and progressing to wider loss.

questions.stem: Which statement about memory across the lifespan is most accurate?
options: All types of memory decline at the same rate from early adulthood onwards
Procedural memory declines first, while episodic memory improves in old age
Memory does not change with age unless a person develops a brain disease
Recall of new information declines in old age; procedural memory is kept
questions.explanation: In normal ageing, episodic memory and the speed of forming new memories tend to decline, while procedural memory and much semantic knowledge are relatively well kept.

questions.stem: In a free recall task of a list of 20 words, the words at the start and end of the list are recalled best. The better recall of the first words is called:
options: the recency effect
proactive interference
chunking
the primacy effect
questions.explanation: The primacy effect is attributed to early items being rehearsed more and transferred to long-term memory. The recency effect occurs because the last items are still in short-term memory.

questions.stem: A researcher reads out a list of 20 words, then has participants do 30 seconds of mental arithmetic before free recall. Compared with immediate recall, what is the most likely result?
options: The recency effect disappears, but the primacy effect remains
The primacy effect disappears, but the recency effect remains
Both effects become stronger because of the extra time to rehearse
Both effects disappear, so all words are recalled equally well
questions.explanation: Counting displaces the last items from short-term memory, removing the recency effect. Early items have already been transferred to long-term memory, so primacy remains.

questions.stem: Most people cannot accurately draw the details on a coin they handle every day. This is best explained as:
options: pseudo-forgetting due to failure to encode
retrograde amnesia due to a head injury
retroactive interference from newer coins
repression of an unpleasant experience
questions.explanation: Pseudo-forgetting is apparent forgetting of information that was never properly encoded, often because it was never attended to. You cannot forget what was never stored.

questions.stem: A student remembers the colours of the rainbow with 'Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain'. This mnemonic is:
options: the peg-word method
an acrostic
an acronym
the method of loci
questions.explanation: An acrostic is a sentence in which the first letter of each word is a cue for an item. An acronym is a single word or abbreviation formed from first letters, such as ROYGBIV.

questions.stem: To remember a speech, a student imagines placing each point at a different spot along her route from her front door to her bedroom. This is:
options: the peg-word method
an acronym
the method of loci
narrative chaining
questions.explanation: The method of loci links each item to a familiar location along a route, then retrieves them by mentally walking the route.

questions.stem: A student memorises 'one is a bun, two is a shoe' and then imagines the first item on a list sitting on a bun. This is:
options: an acrostic
the peg-word method
narrative chaining
the method of loci
questions.explanation: The peg-word method links items to a memorised list of rhyming 'pegs', using vivid images. Narrative chaining links unrelated items into a story.

questions.stem: Why are mnemonics such as narrative chaining effective in improving recall?
options: They keep information in sensory memory until it is needed for recall
They prevent any new learning from interfering with earlier learning
They work by repeating the information until it becomes automatic
They organise and elaborate information, adding retrieval cues
questions.explanation: Mnemonics improve recall by adding organisation, meaning and imagery, which deepens processing and gives more cues for retrieval.
